summary:
Launch Control is a cooperative 3D game in which two players run the operations and launch-readiness stage of a space mission. One player is the astronaut inside the spacecraft cockpit; the other works in mission control. Each sees different information: the astronaut observes and operates the cockpit panel, while mission control reads the procedures manual and uses a calculator. They must talk, share what they know and act together before a shared countdown runs out. Success launches the rocket; a timeout ends in a playful failure.

The game follows NASA's mission segments: the space segment (cockpit), the ground segment (mission control) and the launch segment (the outcome). Like NASA's Mission Design Lab, it shows that missions succeed when specialists combine their knowledge. It offers two difficulty levels and two players connected over a local network.

Our next stage, already designed, brings mission-design trade-offs such as power, communications, propulsion and risk into the same cooperative format. Launch Control makes teamwork part of the mission.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Launch Control is a two-player cooperative game about the operations stage of a space mission. One player is the astronaut in the spacecraft cockpit; the other is mission control in a control room with consoles, a large launch display and a laptop with the procedures manual. Neither player can succeed alone: the astronaut sees the cockpit modules (for example, whether an antenna light is fixed or blinking, or a numeric code) but has no manual; mission control has the procedures and a calculator but cannot touch the controls. They must describe, interpret and confirm actions before a shared countdown ends. Success launches the rocket on both screens; a timeout ends in a playful "cork" failure with a tiny parachute; a lost connection is shown clearly without any explosion.

HOW IT WORKS

Players host or join a session, choose different roles and mark themselves ready. The host validates every attempt, so the interface can never award itself success. Easy difficulty uses one module; normal adds a second module, a matching manual page and a calculator. The countdown, pending modules and result stay visible on a persistent HUD. The interface is available in English and Spanish.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The game makes a key idea of space missions playable: seeing a problem, knowing the procedure and operating the controls belong to different people. It practices precise reporting, listening, instruction-following and shared problem-solving, and it is designed for people with no prior space knowledge, for STEM outreach activities. It is an educational prototype, not flight training, and we have not yet measured learning outcomes.

NASA CONNECTION

We structured the game around the mission segments described in NASA's "Design and Develop Science Missions": the astronaut works in the space segment, mission control in the ground segment, and both decide the launch segment's outcome. NASA's Mission Design Lab inspired the focus on specialists collaborating. Our designed next stage maps new minigames to Mission Design Lab disciplines (communications link margin, power reserve, propulsion and delta-V budget, technical risk, science traceability) to bring mission-design trade-offs into the game. Puzzle rules, numbers and the countdown are our own game mechanics, not NASA procedures or data.

TOOLS

Godot Engine 4.7.2 with GDScript, Godot's ENet networking (host and client), the Compatibility renderer at 1280x720, original 3D geometry built from Godot primitives, and original SVG icons. We used Git and GitHub with continuous integration on Windows and Linux and automated checks for the round logic, the networking and the scenes. On an Intel Core i5 laptop with integrated graphics, it ran at about 60 FPS with both players' windows open.

CREATIVITY

Two very different workstations (a cockpit and a mission-control room), with a live launch view rendered by an in-game camera. Every state is shown with text, icon and color, not color alone. The outcomes are friendly and cartoon-like (pastel smoke, a cork-like nose cone, a parachute) instead of realistic accidents.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility for beginners, readability at 1280x720, clear feedback, fairness (the host validates every action), modest hardware, original assets only (reference photos were used only for analysis), and honest disclosure of AI assistance.
